lessons.title: Climate is not weather

content.intro: If your uncle says 'It was freezing this morning, so much for global warming!' — he's confusing weather with climate. They are not the same thing.

blocks.text: **Weather** is what happens today and this week — rain, sun, a heatwave, a sudden chill. It changes hour to hour.
**Climate** is the long-term pattern over decades — average temperatures, normal rainfall, when monsoons usually arrive. It changes slowly and steadily.
One cold morning doesn't disprove warming. One hot afternoon doesn't prove it. We have to look at 30+ years of data.

India's climate has shifted in measurable ways: monsoons arriving later, heatwaves lasting longer (Delhi crossed 49°C in May 2024), and Himalayan glaciers retreating about 15 metres per year on average.

content.key_takeaway: Weather is your mood today. Climate is your personality over years.
content.mento_says: When someone tries to argue against climate change using today's weather, you'll know it's a category error. That's the start of climate literacy.
content.story_hook: In 2023, India recorded both record-breaking heatwaves AND unusually cold spells in the same year. That's not contradiction — that's a destabilising climate.

lessons.coaching_moment: Climate change shows up as MORE extreme weather of every kind — not just hotter days. Learn to spot the pattern, not the day.

lessons.title: The greenhouse effect, simply

content.intro: The Earth has a blanket made of gases. The blanket is necessary — without it we'd freeze at -18°C on average. The problem is, we keep making the blanket thicker.

blocks.text: Sunlight hits Earth. Some of it bounces back as heat. **Greenhouse gases** (CO₂, methane, water vapor, nitrous oxide) trap that heat in the atmosphere — like a blanket on a winter night.
A *little* blanket is good (it's why Earth is warmer than the Moon, which has the same distance from the Sun but no atmosphere).
A *thick* blanket is bad — it overheats the planet. Since 1850, we've added enough CO₂ to raise global average temperature by 1.2°C.
Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) releases CO₂ that was buried for millions of years. We're undoing millions of years of carbon storage in about 200 years.

content.key_takeaway: The greenhouse effect is natural and necessary. Human-caused thickening of it is the actual problem.
content.mento_says: Climate change isn't 'pollution' the way smog is — it's a slow blanket-thickening that takes decades to feel and centuries to undo. That's what makes it sneaky.
content.story_hook: The greenhouse effect was first described in 1824 by French scientist Joseph Fourier. We've known about this for 200 years — it's not new science.

lessons.coaching_moment: If you can explain the greenhouse effect to a 7-year-old in 30 seconds, you understand it. Try it tonight.

lessons.title: The carbon cycle (and where it broke)

content.intro: Carbon naturally moves in a loop: plants absorb it, animals release it, oceans store it, soil holds it. The loop has worked for millions of years.

blocks.text: **The natural carbon loop**: trees breathe in CO₂ → animals breathe out CO₂ → oceans absorb CO₂ → it all stays balanced.
**What we did**: dug up ancient buried carbon (oil, coal, gas) and burned it, dumping a few hundred million years' worth of carbon into the air in a single century.
**Where it broke**: the natural sinks (forests, oceans) can't keep up. About half of the CO₂ we emit just stays in the atmosphere — for hundreds of years.
We didn't 'create' new carbon. We just released a giant carbon savings account that nature had locked away.

content.key_takeaway: Reading the system as a *cycle* (not a one-way street) is the key climate-thinking skill.
content.mento_says: Imagine your school has a 'borrow a book' system that worked for years. Now imagine somebody comes in and dumps 1000 books on the floor every day. That's us with carbon.

lessons.coaching_moment: Climate is a cycle problem, not a line problem. People who think in cycles will solve this faster.

lessons.title: How climate change is hitting India right now

content.intro: Climate change isn't a polar bear problem in some far-off Arctic. It's already showing up in your city, your food, and your water.

blocks.text: **Heatwaves**: India saw 280+ heatwave days in 2024 (vs. about 30 a decade ago). Construction workers, street vendors, school kids playing outside — everyone is hit.
**Monsoon mess**: Rains arrive 2-3 weeks late, then dump everything in 5 wild days. Farmers in Maharashtra lost crops in 2023 because of this exact pattern.
**Chennai water crisis (2019)**: All four city reservoirs ran dry. People queued for water tankers. This is what climate adaptation actually looks like — chaos at the tap.
**Sinking Sundarbans**: Rising seas are swallowing islands in West Bengal. Families have already relocated as 'climate refugees' — within India.
**Himalayan glaciers**: Retreating fast. The Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Indus depend on them. Slow this down or hundreds of millions face water trouble.
India contributes about 7% of global emissions but is one of the most climate-vulnerable countries. We have to act because we have the most to lose.

content.key_takeaway: Climate change in India isn't future tense. It's present tense.
content.mento_says: When you read the news, train yourself to spot the climate angle. Floods, heatwaves, crop failure, water shortage — most of them now have climate fingerprints.
content.story_hook: In May 2024, a single Delhi day hit 49.9°C. Birds were falling out of the sky from dehydration. That was a wake-up call most of us slept through.

lessons.coaching_moment: Climate change is unfair. The poorest people, who emit the least, are hit the hardest. Remember this every time you discuss it.

lessons.title: Climate Hero Spotlight: Sunita Narain

content.intro: When India's air pollution debate finally became national news, one person had been pushing it for decades. Meet Sunita Narain.

founder_spotlight.name: Sunita Narain
founder_spotlight.company: Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), New Delhi
founder_spotlight.story: Director of CSE since 2002. She's the one who exposed pesticide residues in soft drinks in 2003. She made Delhi switch its public buses to CNG in 2002, cutting pollution massively. She argues — loudly, sharply — that rich countries owe poor countries climate fairness.
founder_spotlight.lesson: Climate science alone doesn't change minds. Climate science + numbers + storytelling + courage does.

blocks.text: Sunita Narain is the reason your auto in Delhi runs on CNG instead of diesel. That single policy change cleaned the air for millions.
She doesn't shy away from naming names — government, corporations, even celebrity influencers — when they greenwash.
She often says: 'Environment is not just about trees. It's about justice.' Climate work IS social work.

content.key_takeaway: Real climate action requires data + courage + persistence. None alone is enough.

lessons.coaching_moment: If you ever doubt that one person can shift national policy — read about Sunita Narain. She did, and is still doing it.

schema.intro: Your carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas you cause through your daily choices. Most of it is invisible. This worksheet makes it visible.

fields.label: How do you usually travel to school?

fields.placeholder: Be honest — say 0 if you're vegetarian, 14+ if you have it daily

fields.placeholder: 0, 4, 8, 12 — your best guess

lessons.title: Field Mission: The Fossil Fuel Hunt
lessons.summary: Walk through your home and find 5+ things that exist because of fossil fuels.

content.intro: Fossil fuels aren't just in petrol pumps. They're hiding in your toothbrush, your shampoo bottle, your sneakers, your school bag. For this mission, walk room by room and find at least 5 items that came from oil, gas, or coal. Take a photo, voice note, or short text for each.

schema.brief: Hunt for 5+ items in your home that are made from or powered by fossil fuels. Plastic, synthetic fabric, electricity-hungry gadgets, vehicles. Note WHY each one is a fossil-fuel item.
persona_prompts: Item 1 — what is it and which fossil fuel is behind it?
Item 4 — bonus: pick a 'surprise' item people don't realise is fossil-based
Item 5 — what's something you could swap for a non-fossil version?

lessons.coaching_moment: Once you start noticing fossil fuels, you'll see them everywhere. That awareness is the first step to changing your defaults.

lessons.title: Reflection: What did the hunt show you?
lessons.instructions: Quick reflection on what surprised you and what feels possible to change.

fields.label: What surprised you most about your fossil-fuel hunt?
fields.placeholder: Maybe how much plastic packaging you found... or that even your school bag is plastic

fields.label: How do you feel after Week 1 — overwhelmed, curious, motivated, anxious?
fields.placeholder: Be honest. All feelings are valid.

fields.label: Name ONE small swap you'd try this month
fields.placeholder: Refill water bottle instead of buying / cycle 2 days a week

lessons.coaching_moment: Climate awareness can feel heavy at first. The cure isn't more guilt — it's small, real action you can stick with.

weeks.title: Community climate decisions
weeks.summary: Real climate problems have trade-offs. Practice making them in Climate Champions and policy worksheets.
weeks.homework_summary: Find one local climate problem in your neighborhood. Write 3 lines on it.

lessons.title: Why climate decisions are hard

content.intro: If shutting down all factories was the obvious answer, we'd have done it. The catch: people work in those factories. Climate decisions are HARD because they're real trade-offs.

blocks.text: Most climate decisions have **three competing pulls**: the planet, the economy, and people's daily lives.
When a city decides to ban old diesel buses, it cleans the air — and *also* makes commuting harder for people who can't afford new vehicles.
When India decides to keep mining coal, it powers electricity for 1.4 billion people — and *also* heats the planet.
A good climate thinker doesn't pretend the trade-offs aren't there. They look at them clearly and pick the option that hurts the *least* and helps the *most*.

content.key_takeaway: Beware of the 'solution that hurts no one'. Usually it's a fantasy.
content.mento_says: Whenever someone proposes a climate solution and says 'this is a win-win for everybody', dig deeper. Real solutions almost always have a cost — and the question is who pays.
content.story_hook: Germany decided to shut down nuclear plants for safety. Result: they had to burn more coal. Climate trade-offs are real. There are no clean answers, only better-than-worse ones.

lessons.coaching_moment: Beware of the 'solution that hurts no one'. Usually it's a fantasy.

lessons.title: Jobs vs environment — the false choice

content.intro: 'You can have jobs OR a clean environment.' This is the most common climate argument — and it's lazy thinking.

blocks.text: **Old story**: Save the trees → factory closes → workers go hungry → environmentalists are 'urban elites' who don't care about real people.
**Real story**: India added 10 million renewable energy jobs in solar and wind in the last decade. Coal jobs are shrinking. Green jobs are growing.
**The real question** isn't 'jobs OR environment'. It's: how do we move workers FROM dying industries (coal, single-use plastic) TO growing ones (solar, EVs, recycling, sustainable farming)?
This is called a 'just transition' — making sure the workers in old fossil industries aren't abandoned as we move to clean energy.

content.key_takeaway: It's not jobs vs environment. It's bad-old-jobs vs better-new-jobs — with a transition plan in between.
content.mento_says: Whenever you hear 'jobs vs environment', ask: which jobs? for how long? and where will the next jobs come from? Usually that flips the conversation.

lessons.coaching_moment: Most 'either-or' framings are emotional traps. Climate progress lives in the AND, with a transition plan.

lessons.title: How climate policy actually works

content.intro: Personal action matters. But the big shifts happen through policy — laws and rules that change what entire industries do. Here's how it works.

cards.title: Bans
cards.body: Outlaw harmful things outright. India banned single-use plastic bags in many states in 2022.

cards.title: Taxes
cards.body: Make harmful things expensive. Petrol tax in India funds road and rail. Carbon taxes make polluters pay.

cards.title: Subsidies
cards.body: Make good things cheap. India subsidises rooftop solar — that's why you see panels everywhere now.

cards.title: Standards
cards.body: Set limits that products must meet. BS-VI emission norms forced cleaner cars on Indian roads in 2020.

content.key_takeaway: Personal habits + good policy = real climate progress. Either alone isn't enough.
content.mento_says: When you read about a climate move in the news, try to spot which lever it pulls — ban, tax, subsidy, or standard. That's policy literacy.
content.story_hook: Switzerland charges drivers a 'gas guzzler' fee on inefficient cars. The cleanest cars get a discount. Result: average new car emissions dropped 30% in 5 years.

lessons.coaching_moment: Personal change is great. Policy change is faster. The smartest climate champions push both.

lessons.title: EVs vs petrol cars — the real story

content.intro: Are electric vehicles really better for the planet? Yes — but the answer is more interesting than it sounds.

blocks.text: Building an EV uses more energy than building a petrol car (because of the battery). So EVs start their life with a 'carbon debt'.
But over their driving life, EVs win — even when charged on India's coal-heavy grid. Why? Petrol cars burn fuel every km. EVs only carry the cost of the electricity they used.
**Break-even**: an EV in India 'pays back' its carbon debt after about 30,000 km. After that, every km is cleaner than petrol.
And as India's grid gets greener (more solar/wind), EVs keep getting cleaner — automatically. Petrol cars don't get that benefit.
EVs aren't magic. They're a step in the right direction — IF the grid keeps cleaning up. Policy and technology have to move together.

content.key_takeaway: Bigger batteries + cleaner grid + recycling = EVs become much greener over time. Petrol can't follow that arc.
content.story_hook: Norway sells more EVs than petrol cars. Their secret: heavy taxes on petrol cars + free parking and toll exemptions for EVs. Policy decided the market.

lessons.coaching_moment: Always ask 'what's the lifecycle?' — not just 'what comes out of the tailpipe today?' That's how you spot real climate winners.

lessons.title: Climate Hero Spotlight: Licypriya Kangujam

content.intro: She started speaking up at age 6. By age 12, she had addressed the United Nations. Meet India's youngest climate activist.

founder_spotlight.name: Licypriya Kangujam
founder_spotlight.story: Born in Manipur in 2011, she addressed the UN Climate Conference at age 8. She has met India's Prime Minister, the UN Secretary-General, and world leaders pushing for stronger climate laws and a mandatory climate education subject in Indian schools.
founder_spotlight.lesson: Age is not a qualification or a barrier. Climate work doesn't wait until you're 'old enough'.

blocks.text: Licypriya was inspired by floods that displaced thousands in Manipur. Climate disaster wasn't a documentary for her — it was her neighbours, her cousins, her school.
She faced criticism: 'too young to understand', 'a parent's mouthpiece'. She kept showing up, kept reading, kept speaking. The criticism faded; the message stayed.
If a 12-year-old can speak at the UN, you can speak in class, in your colony WhatsApp group, in your school assembly. The smaller stages need climate voices too.

content.key_takeaway: Climate leaders don't wait for permission. They start where they are.

lessons.coaching_moment: Your age isn't a reason to stay silent. It might be your superpower — adults underestimate kids, then listen harder when you speak.

schema.intro: Real climate work is local. Pick a problem you can SEE — overflowing drains, heat island, polluted lake, dying tree, smog day. Then think it through like a policy advisor.

lessons.coaching_moment: If your solution has zero trade-offs, you haven't thought hard enough. Real solutions have real costs.

lessons.coaching_moment: The best climate thinkers can defend their choice *and* steelman the other side. That's intellectual honesty.

weeks.title: Waste & circular living
weeks.summary: Reduce > Reuse > Recycle. Plastic, e-waste, composting, and the repair-it culture we forgot.
weeks.homework_summary: For one full day, separate every piece of trash you make into 3 categories.

lessons.title: The 3 R's — but in the right order

content.intro: Recycling is the *last* resort. The first two R's matter way more — and most people get the order wrong.

blocks.text: **Reduce** = don't buy/use it in the first place. (Highest impact — zero energy, zero waste.)
**Reuse** = use it again, in any form. (Second highest — a glass jar that becomes a pencil holder uses no extra energy.)
**Recycle** = break it down and remake it. (Last resort — uses energy, often loses quality.)
If you only ever recycle and never reduce, you're stuck on the slowest fix.

Indian grandmothers got this. The same steel dabba carried tiffin for 30 years. The same milk bottle came back to the dairy. The same newspaper became wrapping paper, then fire kindling, then ash for the garden.

content.key_takeaway: The fastest climate action is often the one you *don't* take — the purchase you skip.
content.mento_says: Next time you're about to buy something, run the 3 R's backwards. Can I recycle what I have? Can I reuse what I have? Can I just NOT buy this? Often the answer is yes.

lessons.coaching_moment: Recycling is often a guilt-relief tool, not a climate fix. Reduce is where real impact lives.

lessons.title: The plastic problem (it's bigger than you think)

content.intro: India generates about 9 million tonnes of plastic waste per year. Less than 30% is properly recycled. The rest goes to landfills, drains, beaches, and eventually the ocean — and our food.

blocks.text: **Microplastics**: Plastic doesn't biodegrade. It just breaks into smaller pieces — microplastics — that end up in fish, salt, drinking water, and even human blood.

**Multi-layer packaging**: The shiny chips packets and biscuit wrappers? They're 4-5 different plastics fused together. Almost impossible to recycle. Most go to landfill or are burnt (releasing toxic fumes).
**Single-use is the worst kind**: A plastic straw is used for 10 minutes and lasts 500 years in nature. The math doesn't make sense.
The Ganges and Indus are among the top 10 plastic-polluting rivers in the world. Plastic from your colony eventually reaches the sea.

content.key_takeaway: The plastic problem isn't 'somewhere else'. It's in your house, your tiffin, your tap water. And every cut helps.
content.story_hook: In 2019, India banned single-use plastic in 25 categories. Implementation has been mixed — but states like Sikkim and Tamil Nadu have shown it can work with political will.

lessons.coaching_moment: Once you see microplastics in your salt, you can't un-see it. But you CAN choose less plastic going forward.

lessons.title: E-waste: the trash you don't see

content.intro: Every old phone, dead headphone, broken charger, busted laptop — that's e-waste. India generates 3.2 million tonnes of it per year. Almost none gets properly handled.

blocks.text: **Why it matters**: E-waste contains heavy metals like lead, mercury, and cadmium. When it leaks into soil and water, it poisons farms and groundwater for decades.
**Where it goes**: Most informal recyclers in India break it down by hand — workers, often kids, breathe toxic fumes for ₹200/day. That's an environmental AND human rights issue.
**What you can do**: Don't throw old electronics in regular trash. India has authorized e-waste collectors. Check if your phone brand has a take-back programme (Apple, Samsung, Mi all do).
The longer you keep one phone, the less e-waste you create. Resist the new-model itch — it's the cheapest climate action you can take.

content.key_takeaway: Electronics aren't 'just trash' — they're toxic, valuable, and worth handling properly.
content.mento_says: Look around your house. Count the dead chargers, old phones, broken earphones in drawers. That's your personal e-waste pile. Find an authorised collector this month.

lessons.coaching_moment: Phone upgrade pressure is engineered. Slowing down your upgrade cycle is one of the fastest things you can do for the climate.

lessons.title: Composting and the lost art of repair

content.intro: Two huge climate fixes are quietly hiding in plain sight: composting your kitchen waste, and learning to repair things instead of replacing them.

blocks.text: **Composting**: 50%+ of household trash is food waste. In a landfill, it rots without oxygen and produces methane (28x worse than CO₂). In a compost bin, it becomes free fertiliser for plants.
**Apartment composting works**: A small bin (₹500), a corner of your balcony, and 3 weeks. That's it. No smell if done right.
**Repair culture**: Your grandparents took shoes to a cobbler, mended clothes, repaired umbrellas. Each repair = one less new product needed.
**Repair Cafes** are now starting in Indian cities — community spaces where you bring broken stuff and learn to fix it. Bangalore, Pune, and Delhi have active ones.
The most climate-friendly thing in your house is the thing you already own. Use it longer, fix it when it breaks, pass it on when you're done.

content.key_takeaway: Composting + repair = circular living. It's how humans lived for thousands of years before we forgot.
content.story_hook: Sweden recycles 99% of household waste. Their secret? They tax landfilling, subsidise repair, and make composting mandatory. Policy + culture, working together.

lessons.coaching_moment: Repair is rebellion. Every fix is a tiny vote against the throw-away economy.

lessons.title: Climate Hero Spotlight: Afroz Shah

content.intro: In 2015, one Mumbai lawyer looked at Versova Beach — buried under 5 feet of plastic — and decided to clean it. Just him and a neighbour. They became a global movement.

founder_spotlight.name: Afroz Shah
founder_spotlight.story: Mumbai lawyer who started cleaning Versova Beach in October 2015 with his elderly neighbour. Volunteers grew week by week. By 2018, they'd removed 5 million kg of plastic. Olive Ridley turtles returned to nest on the beach in 2018 for the first time in 20 years.
founder_spotlight.lesson: Don't wait for a campaign. Start cleaning the corner you can see. Others will join.

blocks.text: Afroz Shah didn't have a budget, an NGO, or a media team. He had a beach, gloves, and stubbornness. The UN named him a 'Champion of the Earth' in 2016.
He's clear-eyed about what works: 'Cleaning is only step one. The real fix is stopping plastic from reaching the beach in the first place.' He now works on awareness, source-control, and policy too.
Showing up every weekend for 9 years — that's the secret. Climate action is mostly persistence, not heroism.

content.key_takeaway: You don't need a movement to start. Start, and the movement comes.

lessons.coaching_moment: If you're waiting for the 'right time' to start climate work, you'll wait forever. Pick a small corner this weekend.

lessons.title: Play: Eco Warrior — Sort to Save the Planet
lessons.context: Speed-sort items into compost / recycle / landfill / hazardous. See how fast (and accurate) you really are.
lessons.coaching_moment: Watch which category you mis-sort the most — that's your real-world recycling blind spot.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Find one thing to swap
lessons.instructions: Pick ONE item you use that's high-waste, and design a low-waste replacement.

schema.title: Your circular swap
schema.intro: Don't try to fix everything. Pick ONE item, do the math, design a swap, and commit.

fields.label: What's the wasteful item?
fields.placeholder: Plastic water bottles I keep buying / chip packets / paper towels

fields.label: How many do you use per week?
fields.placeholder: Be honest — best estimate is fine

fields.label: Multiply by 52. That's your yearly waste in this category. Write the number.
fields.placeholder: Example: 5 bottles/week × 52 = 260 bottles/year

fields.label: What's a low-waste swap?
fields.placeholder: Steel water bottle + filter at home / make snack at home / cloth napkin

fields.label: What's the REAL reason you haven't swapped yet?
fields.placeholder: Be honest — laziness, cost, social, forgot, taste...

fields.label: What's the smallest first step you can take this week?
fields.placeholder: Buy the steel bottle / borrow one / set a phone reminder

lessons.coaching_moment: Most 'I can't' really means 'I haven't tried yet'. The honest answer is half the swap.

lessons.title: Field Mission: Trash Audit
lessons.summary: For ONE day, log every piece of trash you create. Tag each one — REDUCE, REUSE, RECYCLE, or NONE.

content.intro: An audit is a mirror. Most people are surprised by what shows up. For one full day, write down (or photograph) every piece of trash that leaves your hand — packets, bottles, paper, peels, anything. Then tag each item: REDUCE (could've avoided it), REUSE (could've reused), RECYCLE (recyclable), NONE (true landfill). Aim for at least 10 items. The truth will surprise you.

schema.brief: For 1 full day, log every piece of trash you create. Tag each item with the best 'R' for it. Aim for 10+ items.
persona_prompts: Item 1 — what is it? Best R for it?
Item 4 — bonus: was there a 'sneaky' item you almost didn't count?

lessons.coaching_moment: An audit is a mirror. Most people are surprised by what shows up. Don't judge — just notice.

lessons.title: Week 3 Checkpoint

fields.question: Which has the BIGGEST climate impact?

options.label: Reducing what you buy in the first place

fields.explanation: Less consumption beats every kind of disposal.

fields.question: Which item is hardest to recycle?
fields.explanation: Multi-layer plastics are extremely hard to separate; most go to landfill.

fields.question: 'Greenwashing' means:

options.label: Cleaning a product with eco-friendly soap
A company pretending to be sustainable to sell more

fields.explanation: Greenwashing = marketing that looks eco-friendly without actually being so.

fields.question: Why is composting important for climate?

options.label: Food waste in landfills releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas

fields.explanation: Methane from rotting food is 28x more warming than CO₂. Composting prevents this.

fields.question: Why is e-waste especially dangerous?

options.label: It contains toxic heavy metals that leak into soil and water
It looks ugly in the bin

fields.explanation: Lead, mercury, and cadmium can poison groundwater and farms for decades.

fields.question: Afroz Shah is famous for:

options.label: Cleaning Mumbai's Versova Beach with weekly volunteer effort

fields.explanation: His Versova Beach Clean-Up became one of the world's largest community-led cleanup movements.

fields.question: Order the 3 R's by climate impact (highest first):
fields.explanation: Not buying it (Reduce) is the most powerful. Recycling is a last-resort fix.

lessons.coaching_moment: Spotting greenwashing is a superpower. Always ask: what's the hard number?

points: Reduce > Reuse > Recycle — in that order, always
Plastic doesn't biodegrade; multi-layer packaging is nearly impossible to recycle
E-waste is toxic, valuable, and almost always handled wrong
Composting + repair are forgotten climate superpowers
Afroz Shah proves: small consistent action beats big plans
week_recap.try_this: This week, set up one composting attempt — even a small bucket on the balcony. Or take 1 broken thing to a repair shop instead of replacing it.

weeks.title: Ecosystems & your action plan
weeks.summary: Biodiversity, ecosystem services, tipping points, climate justice, and your real action pledge.
weeks.homework_summary: Make your climate action pledge real — share it with at least 1 friend or family member.

lessons.title: Biodiversity — why species matter

content.intro: Biodiversity is the variety of life — plants, animals, fungi, microbes. India has 8% of all species in the world, on just 2.4% of the land. We are a biodiversity superpower.

blocks.text: **Why we should care**: every species is part of a web. Bees pollinate crops (one in three bites of food depends on pollinators). Vultures clean dead animals (when India lost most of its vultures, dog and rat populations exploded — and so did rabies).
**The Sixth Extinction**: we're losing species 1000x faster than the natural rate. The current extinction wave is being caused by humans — habitat loss, pollution, climate change.
**India's stories**: tigers came back from 1,400 in 2006 to 3,600+ in 2022 thanks to Project Tiger. Bees are vanishing in many regions because of pesticides and shrinking flowering plants.
Healthy biodiversity isn't a luxury. It's the operating system of nature. Lose enough pieces and the whole thing crashes.

content.key_takeaway: Every species lost is a thread pulled from a giant tapestry. Pull enough threads, and the picture falls apart.
content.story_hook: When wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995, the rivers literally changed course. Wolves ate too-many deer → trees grew back → riverbanks stabilised → rivers shifted. ONE species moved EVERYTHING.

lessons.coaching_moment: When you protect ONE species, you often protect dozens of others. That's the gift of seeing the web.

lessons.title: Play: Ecosystem Explorer
lessons.context: Step into a living forest. See what happens when you remove a species, add a predator, or change the temperature.
lessons.coaching_moment: Healthy ecosystems aren't 'balanced' — they're constantly self-correcting. Watch the feedback loops.

lessons.title: Ecosystem services — the free things nature does

content.intro: Forests don't send you a bill, but they save you money. Bees don't ask for a salary, but they keep food affordable. These are 'ecosystem services' — and they're worth trillions.

cards.title: Water filtering
cards.body: Forests and wetlands clean water for free. Mumbai's Sanjay Gandhi National Park supplies 30% of the city's water.

cards.title: Air cleaning
cards.body: Trees and oceans absorb CO₂. The Amazon rainforest produces about 6% of the world's oxygen.

cards.title: Pollination
cards.body: Bees, butterflies, and bats pollinate one-third of all human food crops — for free.

cards.title: Flood control
cards.body: Mangroves and forests slow floods. Sundarbans saved Kolkata from worse damage during Cyclone Amphan in 2020.

content.key_takeaway: Nature's free services are worth more than every economy on Earth combined. We just don't see the bill — until they're gone.
content.mento_says: Whenever you're near a tree, river, or beach, ask: 'what's the free service this is doing for my city right now?' The answer is usually shocking.
content.story_hook: Cape Town nearly ran out of water in 2018 ('Day Zero'). The fix included restoring upstream wetlands. Nature was the cheapest infrastructure.

lessons.coaching_moment: If a city pays ₹100 crore for a water plant when an upstream forest could've done it for free — that's a planning failure, not a money problem.

lessons.title: Tipping points (and why they're scary)

content.intro: Some climate changes are gradual. Others, once they start, can't be stopped. These are tipping points — and they're the scariest part of climate science.

blocks.text: **A tipping point** is when a system changes state — like an ice cube melting, or a forest turning into grassland. After that point, going back is *very* hard.
**Examples we're watching**: Arctic ice melt (almost gone in summers by 2050), Amazon rainforest dieback (could turn into savannah), coral bleaching (50%+ of Great Barrier Reef already dead).
**Why nonlinear is scary**: most things change a little, then a little more. Tipping points are different. They look stable — until they suddenly aren't.
This is why climate scientists care so much about staying below 1.5°C — past it, several tipping points may trigger together. That's a cascade.

content.key_takeaway: Most systems are forgiving — until suddenly they aren't. That's a tipping point.
content.mento_says: If you've ever stacked blocks until they fall, you know what nonlinear means. The 9th block didn't 'cause' the fall — every block contributed. Climate is the same.
content.story_hook: The West Antarctic ice sheet may already be past its tipping point. Even if we stopped emissions today, it might still collapse — over centuries — adding 3 metres to global sea levels.

lessons.coaching_moment: Most systems are forgiving — until suddenly they aren't. That's why ACTING NOW matters. Acting after = much harder.

lessons.title: Climate justice — who pays, who suffers

content.intro: The countries that caused most of the climate crisis are not the ones suffering most. That's why climate isn't just a science problem — it's a justice problem.

blocks.text: **The math**: rich countries (USA, EU, UK) are responsible for over 60% of historical emissions. They have just 15% of the world's people.
**The hit**: poorer countries (Bangladesh, Pacific Islands, parts of Africa, parts of India) face the worst floods, heat, and crop failures — even though they emitted very little.
**Within India too**: a daily-wage worker on a Delhi construction site at 47°C suffers far more than a child in an air-conditioned classroom. Climate inequality is in the same city.
**The fight**: countries like India argue that rich nations should pay 'climate finance' to help vulnerable countries adapt. The COP climate conferences are essentially long arguments about this.
Climate justice isn't just charity. It's the recognition that whoever broke the system should help fix it.

content.key_takeaway: Climate is a fairness issue as much as it is a science issue. Both lenses matter.
content.story_hook: In 2022, Pakistan suffered floods that submerged a third of the country. Pakistan's emissions are less than 1% of the global total. Whose fault was it? That question is climate justice.

lessons.coaching_moment: When you advocate for climate, you're also advocating for fairness. They can't be separated — and you should never let anyone pretend they can.

lessons.title: Climate Hero Spotlight: Vandana Shiva

content.intro: She walked away from a physics PhD to become a farmer-scientist. She's now one of the loudest voices in the world for seed sovereignty, organic farming, and climate justice.

founder_spotlight.name: Vandana Shiva
founder_spotlight.story: Trained as a quantum physicist. Founded Navdanya in 1987 to save India's traditional seed varieties from being lost to industrial agriculture. Today Navdanya has saved over 2,000 rice varieties and trained more than 900,000 farmers in organic, climate-resilient farming.
founder_spotlight.lesson: Saving seeds isn't nostalgia. It's climate insurance — diverse seeds survive floods, droughts, pests when modern monoculture crops fail.

blocks.text: She points out: when farmers grow only one type of rice, one disease can wipe out the whole crop. Diversity = resilience.
She also takes on huge agricultural corporations who patent seeds. 'Nobody owns nature,' she says. 'You can't patent what billions of farmers gave the world for free.'
Vandana Shiva's work shows: climate solutions live in farms, kitchens, and traditional knowledge — not just in labs and policy halls.

content.key_takeaway: Climate resilience grows from the ground up — literally.

lessons.coaching_moment: Talk to a farmer this year if you can. They've been doing climate adaptation for generations — without using the word.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Your personal climate action plan
lessons.instructions: Map your action plan across 4 zones: home, school, neighbourhood, and online voice.

schema.title: Your 4-zone climate action plan
schema.intro: Real action lives in specific places. Pick at least one move in each zone — and aim for things you'll actually do, not things that sound good.

fields.label: ZONE 1 — Home: one habit you'll change at home this month
fields.placeholder: Compost kitchen waste / cut AC use to 6 hours / no AC at night

fields.label: ZONE 2 — School: one thing you'll push at school
fields.placeholder: Start a recycling bin / persuade canteen to drop plastic / start a green club

fields.label: ZONE 3 — Neighbourhood: one thing you'll do in your colony
fields.placeholder: Tree-planting drive / cleanup of one street / talk to RWA about composting

fields.label: ZONE 4 — Voice: how will you talk about climate?
fields.placeholder: Post one thoughtful thing per week / debate your uncle / give a class presentation

fields.label: What's the biggest obstacle that might stop you?
fields.placeholder: Be honest — laziness, parents, no time, social pressure, money

fields.label: What's the smallest action you'll do in the first 30 days?
fields.placeholder: ONE specific thing you'll actually do

lessons.coaching_moment: Action plans without specific dates and locations are just wishlists. Specific + local + small = real change.

lessons.title: Reflection: Your climate action pledge
lessons.instructions: Three real, doable commitments. No vague promises.

schema.title: My climate action pledge
schema.intro: A vague pledge is a broken pledge. Specific + small + accountable wins. Lock in your three commitments here.

fields.label: Pledge 1 — something you'll START (specific!)
fields.placeholder: Carry a steel bottle every day instead of buying water

fields.label: Pledge 2 — something you'll STOP
fields.placeholder: Stop buying snack packets in single-use plastic

fields.label: Pledge 3 — something you'll TEACH someone else
fields.placeholder: Teach my younger cousin to sort waste

fields.label: Who will hold you accountable? (Friend / family / yourself)
fields.placeholder: Name them. Tell them this week.

fields.label: When will you review your progress?
fields.placeholder: End of every month — set a phone reminder

fields.label: Why does this matter to you, in your own words?
fields.placeholder: When you're 30, what world do you want to be living in?

lessons.coaching_moment: A vague pledge is a broken pledge. Specific + small + accountable wins. Read your pledge out loud once a week.

lessons.title: Final Assessment — Climate Champions
lessons.instructions: Score 70%+ to earn your Climate Champion certificate.

fields.question: Which trio of greenhouse gases matters MOST for climate change?
fields.explanation: These three trap the most heat in the atmosphere.

fields.question: Best definition of 'sustainability':

options.label: Meeting today's needs without breaking tomorrow's

fields.explanation: Classic Brundtland definition — across generations.

options.label: Livestock farms use lots of land and water

fields.explanation: Both methane emissions AND land/water use add up.

fields.question: Climate tipping point means:

options.label: A small change you can reverse easily
A threshold past which a system shifts state and won't bounce back
When a tree falls in a forest

fields.explanation: Once past, recovery takes centuries — or never.

fields.question: The MOST powerful long-term climate action a young person can take is:

options.label: Voting / advocating for systemic policy change

fields.explanation: Individual swaps matter, but systems shift fastest through collective advocacy.

fields.question: 'Ecosystem services' refers to:

options.label: The free benefits nature provides — water filtering, pollination, flood control

fields.explanation: These services are worth trillions — but invisible until they're lost.

fields.question: Climate justice means:

options.label: Recognising that those who emit least often suffer most, and helping them adapt

fields.explanation: It's about fairness, accountability, and support — not just punishment.

fields.question: Vandana Shiva is best known for:

options.label: Saving India's traditional seed varieties through Navdanya

fields.explanation: Her work on seed sovereignty has trained nearly a million farmers in organic, climate-resilient agriculture.

lessons.coaching_moment: If you scored 70%+ you've earned your Climate Champion title — go use it. If not, review the lessons and try again. The world needs you.

points: Biodiversity is nature's safety net — every species lost weakens it
Ecosystem services (water, pollination, flood control) are free and priceless
Tipping points: most damage hides in nonlinear, sudden shifts
Climate justice: those who polluted least often suffer most
Real action lives in 4 zones: home, school, neighbourhood, voice
